title: Symmetric Tree
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether a binary tree is symmetric around its center. Each left subtree must mirror the corresponding right subtree in both structure and values.
Idea: Compare two nodes as a mirror pair. Both null means equal; exactly one null or unequal values means false; otherwise compare left-left against right-right and left-right against right-left.
Technique and why it applies: Mirror symmetry swaps left and right relationships at every level, so paired recursion checks the exact structural condition.
Invariant: A recursive mirror check is true only if the two subtrees are mirror images.
Edge cases: An empty tree is symmetric. Equal values alone are insufficient if child positions differ.
Complexity: Time is O(n), since each node is checked once. Extra space is O(h) for recursion depth.
complexity_reason: Each mirrored node pair is compared once.

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
approach_name: Queue one level at a time
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the values of a binary tree grouped by depth, scanning each level from left to right.
Idea: Use a queue. At the start of each outer iteration, capture the queue size, process exactly that many nodes into one level list, and enqueue their children.
Technique and why it applies: Breadth-first traversal naturally visits nodes in increasing depth order, and the captured queue size separates levels.
Invariant: Before a level is processed, the queue contains exactly the nodes at that depth in left-to-right order.
Edge cases: An empty tree returns an empty list. Enqueue left child before right child to preserve left-to-right order.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(w), where w is the maximum tree width.
complexity_reason: Each node is enqueued and removed once; the queue holds at most one level.

title: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal
notes:
Task and constraints: Return tree values level by level, alternating left-to-right and right-to-left order.
Idea: Perform ordinary breadth-first traversal and collect each level. Reverse every other level before appending it to the result, while still enqueuing children left-to-right.
Technique and why it applies: The zigzag requirement changes only the output order within each level, not which nodes belong to the next level.
Invariant: The queue always represents the next level in ordinary left-to-right order, independent of how the current level is output.
Edge cases: The root level has one value. A one-child level looks the same in either direction.
Complexity: Time is O(n), including level reversals. Extra space is O(w) for the queue and current level, excluding output.
complexity_reason: Breadth-first traversal visits each node once; each level is reversed at most once.

title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the number of nodes on the longest path from the root to a leaf. An empty tree has depth zero.
Idea: Recursively compute the depth of the left and right subtrees and return one plus their maximum.
Technique and why it applies: The deepest root-to-leaf path must descend into one of the two child subtrees, so the larger child depth determines the result.
Invariant: Each recursive result is the maximum depth of the subtree rooted at its argument.
Edge cases: A leaf returns one; a missing child contributes depth zero.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(h) for recursion depth.
complexity_reason: Every node is visited once, with recursion depth equal to tree height.

title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
approach_name: Use preorder root and inorder split
notes:
Task and constraints: Reconstruct a binary tree from preorder and inorder traversals containing unique values.
Idea: The next preorder value is the subtree root. Find its index in inorder; values to its left form the left subtree and values to its right form the right subtree. Recurse on those ranges.
Technique and why it applies: Preorder visits root first, while inorder identifies the exact boundary between left and right subtrees.
Invariant: Each recursive call builds the unique tree for its paired traversal ranges, and the preorder index advances in root-left-right order.
Edge cases: Empty ranges return null. A value-to-index map avoids scanning the inorder range at every recursive step.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(n) for the index map and recursion.
complexity_reason: Each value is consumed once and the inorder map gives constant-expected-time splits.

title: Construct Binary Tree from Inorder and Postorder Traversal
approach_name: Use postorder root and inorder split
notes:
Task and constraints: Reconstruct a binary tree from inorder and postorder traversals containing unique values.
Idea: The last unused postorder value is the root. Find it in inorder, then build the right subtree before the left subtree because postorder is consumed backward.
Technique and why it applies: Postorder visits left, right, root; reverse consumption visits root, right, left, so recursion must follow that order.
Invariant: The postorder index points to the last unconsumed node in the current subtree, and the inorder range defines its descendants.
Edge cases: Empty ranges return null. A value-to-index map avoids repeated linear scans.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(n) for the map and recursion.
complexity_reason: Each value is consumed once and the inorder map gives constant-expected-time splits.

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal II
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the level-order traversal from the leaf level up to the root, preserving left-to-right order within each level.
Idea: Use breadth-first traversal to collect ordinary top-down levels, then reverse the list of levels.
Technique and why it applies: BFS already identifies level boundaries; reversing only the outer list changes the level order without changing node order within each level.
Invariant: Each collected level contains exactly the nodes at one depth in left-to-right order.
Edge cases: Empty input returns an empty list. A one-node tree returns a single one-element level.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(w) for the queue, aside from the returned levels.
complexity_reason: Every node is visited once and the list of levels is reversed once.

title: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree
notes:
Task and constraints: Convert an ascending sorted array into a height-balanced binary search tree.
Idea: Choose the midpoint of the current array range as root, then recursively build left and right subtrees from the halves.
Technique and why it applies: The midpoint minimizes the size difference between left and right subarrays, producing a height-balanced BST while preserving sorted order.
Invariant: Each recursive subtree contains exactly the values in its range and satisfies BST ordering.
Edge cases: Empty ranges return null. Either middle choice is valid for even-length ranges if used consistently.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each value becomes one node. Recursion space is O(log n) for a balanced tree.
space_complexity: O(log n) recursion for a balanced result
complexity_reason: Each array element becomes one node and the midpoint halves each range.

title: Convert Sorted List to Binary Search Tree
approach_name: Copy list values then build balanced BST
notes:
Task and constraints: Convert an ascending sorted linked list into a height-balanced BST.
Idea: Copy list values into an array, then apply the sorted-array midpoint construction to that array.
Technique and why it applies: The array provides constant-time midpoint access, allowing each recursive split to create a balanced tree without repeatedly scanning the list.
Invariant: Each recursive array range contains exactly the sorted values assigned to its subtree, so midpoint selection preserves BST order.
Edge cases: An empty list returns null. A one-node list becomes a single-node tree.
Complexity: Time is O(n) to copy and build. Extra space is O(n) for the array plus recursion.
space_complexity: O(n) for copied values plus recursion
complexity_reason: The linked list is traversed once to create an indexed array, then each value is used once.

title: Balanced Binary Tree
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether every node's left and right subtree heights differ by at most one.
Idea: Recursively compute subtree heights. Return a negative sentinel as soon as a subtree is unbalanced; otherwise return one plus the larger child height.
Technique and why it applies: Combining height calculation and balance detection in one postorder traversal avoids recomputing heights for every node.
Invariant: A non-negative return value is the subtree height if balanced; a negative value means imbalance exists below.
Edge cases: Empty trees are balanced with height zero. A long one-sided chain becomes unbalanced once its height difference exceeds one.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(h) for recursion.
complexity_reason: Each subtree height is computed once and imbalance propagates upward.
